Also any guidance on testing documents with real users.

content.content:
# Plain Language Guidance Summary

## Federal Definition
The webpage indicates that plain language means content that is "clear and easy to understand," designed so the public can grasp their obligations and benefits.

## Legal Requirement
"The Plain Writing Act of 2010 established the requirement that content for the public is written for its specific audience."

## Three-Part Test
Unfortunately, the webpage does not explicitly present a three-part test with the specific structure you mentioned (find/understand/use). However, it does reference four featured guides addressing related concepts:
- Principles of plain language
- Writing for understanding
- Design for understanding  
- Test for understanding

## User Testing Guidance
The page mentions "Learn how to test that your content is easily understandable" under the "Test for understanding" section, but specific testing methodologies with real users are not detailed in this excerpt. The guide appears to be an entry point directing readers to explore more detailed guidance in the linked sections.

For comprehensive information on the three-part test and user testing protocols, you would need to consult the full guides themselves.

# Architecture principles

## What this set governs

This is the architecture-scope principle set: the standing rules for how
the product is designed — its regions, their boundaries, and the entities
that build and evolve them. It is a peer of the working-scope set,
[Founding principles](principles.md), which governs how every activity is
performed; this set governs what the designed system must look like.
Backticked slugs cite principles; a slug not defined in this document is
defined in the working set. The terms Bounded Context, shop, activity,
contract, relationship kind, and intent are defined in the
[glossary](glossary.md). Two distinctions those terms carry are used
throughout. A shop is either the lead shop — the system-level
coordinator, owning the product-level artifacts and no Bounded
Context — or a BC-shop, owning exactly one. A contract is offered
either as a product contract, on a Bounded Context, or as an
operational contract, on a shop.

Where a principle here applies a working-scope principle at the
architecture level, this document declares the lineage in its
frontmatter — `derives-from` maps the principle in this set to the
working-scope principle it applies — instead of restating the rule as a
second authority.

## What a good principle looks like

This section restates the shared definition from the
[principle-set typedef](artifacts/principle-set.md) so this document can
be read alone; the restatement is a rendering, not a second authority.

A principle is a standing rule, in four parts: a name, a statement, a
rationale, and implications.

- The **statement** is the rule. It carries the only normative keywords
  (MUST, SHOULD, MAY — interpreted per BCP 14 when, and only when, they
  appear in capitals) and is testable: shown a piece of work, you can
  answer yes or no. A statement carrying more than one obligation
  presents one obligation per bullet.
- The **rationale** says why the rule earns its place: the failure it
  prevents, shown as a generic example; well-known external references
  may support it, the product's own history never appears. Rationales
  stay prose.
- The **implications** are the price tag: one implication per bullet,
  the concrete change each named actor absorbs to honor the rule. They
  add no obligations — every implication must be derivable from the
  statement, or it is a misfiled rule.

A principle is good when its statement is testable (TOGAF, The Open
Group Architecture Framework: understandable, complete, consistent), it
rejects work we would otherwise do (Jared Spool, "Creating Great Design
Principles"), it directs without prescribing method (Richard Rumelt,
*Good Strategy Bad Strategy*), it is not a claim every shop would make
(Patrick Lencioni, "Make Your Values Mean Something", Harvard Business
Review, 2002), and it implies at least one practice and one check. The fitness screen at the
end of this document applies these tests to the principles above it.

---

## Every first-class entity has a knowable shape (`knowable-shape`)

**Statement.**

- The product MUST have exactly two kinds of first-class entity: the
  Bounded Context and the shop.
- Each Bounded Context MUST be contained and produced by exactly one
  BC-shop; the lead shop MUST NOT contain one.
- Every first-class entity MUST carry a description, maintained as an
  artifact, from which an outside reader can name what the entity is
  for, what it accepts and produces, what it guarantees, and the
  contracts it offers.
- The description MUST suffice without reading the entity's internal
  code or configuration and without asking its maintainers.

**Rationale.** When an entity's shape lives only in its internals, every
consumer, coordinator, and reviewer pays to rediscover it, and each
rediscovery reaches a different answer: nobody can say what a service
guarantees without opening its source, the answer holds only until the
next commit, and no description can be trusted without re-inspecting
the thing it describes. Parnas made the design case in 1972: a module
is known by what its interface states, not by what its implementation
happens to do. Without `knowable-shape`,
`contracts-between-contexts` is speculative — no one can write a
contract for an entity whose shape no one can state.

**Implications.**

- Whoever creates a Bounded Context or a shop writes its description at
  creation; an entity without a description is not yet created,
  whatever code exists.
- Maintainers keep the description authoritative: when an outside
  reader must open internals to answer a question the description
  claims to cover, the description is the defect and its maintainer
  repairs it.
- Architects reason from descriptions; opening an entity's internals is
  audit work — checking that a description is true — not the normal way
  to learn what the entity is.

## Contracts are the only channel between Bounded Contexts (`contracts-between-contexts`)

**Statement.**

- Anything one Bounded Context expects of another MUST pass through a
  named, versioned contract stating the schemas exchanged, the meaning
  of each operation, the error behavior, and the relationship kind.
- A Bounded Context MUST NOT rely on anything its counterpart's

# Guideline: principle set

**Voice principle.** Write for the reviewer who must accept or reject a
piece of work against the rule tomorrow: every sentence binds, evidences,
or prices — nothing decorates.

**Highlights (the layer compiled into generating context):** statement
decidable yes/no on one piece of work · normative keywords in statements
only · rationale shows a generic failure, never the product's operational
history ·
implications name the actor who absorbs the price · one obligation or
implication per bullet; rationales stay prose · what the principle
rejects lives inside the four parts · cite principles by slug, never by
number.

**Layers:** this guideline adds principle-set rules on top of the
[base writing style](base-writing-style.md); the base always applies and
is never overridden. When rules conflict, an approved principle beats the
[principle-set typedef](../artifacts/principle-set.md), which beats this
guideline.

---

## Rules

**1. Make the statement decidable on one piece of work.**
Before: "Contracts matter and should generally be respected across
boundaries."
After: "Anything one context expects of another MUST pass through a
named, versioned contract."
*Test:* hold one concrete piece of work against the statement alone.
*Criterion:* a reviewer can answer yes or no without reading the
rationale or implications. *Decision:* yes/no per statement.
*Derived check:* judged — scenario 2 of
[principle-set.fitness.md](../fitness/principle-set.fitness.md).

**2. Confine normative keywords to statements.**
Before: "Implication: reviewers MUST delete unlinked checks."
After: "Implication: reviewers delete unlinked checks."
*Test:* scan for BCP 14 capitals. *Criterion:* capitals outside
statements appear only in the opening's keyword-definition sentence
(mentions, not uses). *Decision:* yes/no per occurrence.
*Derived check:* mechanical — the grep row of the principle-set typedef's
derived review checklist.

**3. Ground the rationale in a generic failure, never product history.**
Before: "Decision 12 (2026-08-14, the incident review) named this
exact failure."
After: "A consumer that copies a schema instead of referencing it
drifts from the real schema within days."
*Test:* read each rationale. *Criterion:* it names the failure the rule
prevents with a generic example any reader can recognize without knowing
our history; it references no operational history of the product —
artifacts, issues, incidents, decision records, counts; a well-known external
reference (a published work, a standard, a named law) may support it.
*Decision:* yes/no per rationale.
*Derived check:* judged — fitness scenario 3.

**4. Price implications on a named actor.**
Before: "Care must be taken to keep renderings consistent."
After: "Only the compiler touches renderings; a hand edit to a rendering
is reverted, not merged."
*Test:* parse each implication. *Criterion:* it names the actor who
absorbs the change, follows from a statement clause, and adds no
obligation the statement does not carry. *Decision:* yes/no per
implication.
*Derived check:* judged — fitness scenario 4, and the typedef's
traceability row.

**5. Keep rejections inside the four parts.**
Before: a free-standing "**Anti-pattern ruled out.** Two contexts that
'just know' how to interact." block after the implications.
After: the same failure carried in the rationale, or priced in an
implication — no fifth part.
*Test:* list every element of each principle. *Criterion:* only the four
parts appear, and what the principle rules out is stated inside them.
*Decision:* yes/no per principle.
*Derived check:* judged — fitness scenario 1.

**6. Cite a principle by its slug.**
Before: "Without Principle 2, Principle 4 collapses."
After: "Without `single-source-of-truth`, renderings drift."
*Test:* scan cross-references to principles, inside the set and in
documents citing it. *Criterion:* each reference uses the kebab-case
slug, never a number or a position. *Decision:* yes/no per reference.
*Derived check:* judged — fitness scenario 1's slug-citation assertion;
a mechanical reference lint is possible later and is listed as a
chain-review item, not assumed.

**7. Give each obligation its own bullet.**
Before: "Anything one context expects of another MUST pass through a
named, versioned contract, and a context MUST NOT rely on anything the
contract does not state, and contexts MUST NOT coordinate outside it."
After: "- Anything one context expects of another MUST pass through a
named, versioned contract. / - A context MUST NOT rely on anything the
contract does not state." (as a real bulleted list)
*Test:* list each statement's obligations and its bullets; parse each
implications block. *Criterion:* a statement carrying more than one
obligation presents one obligation per bullet, with conditional logic
kept inside its bullet; a single-obligation statement stays one
sentence; implications list one implication per bullet; rationales stay
prose; enumerations state whether they are closed. *Decision:* yes/no
per principle.
*Derived check:* judged — fitness scenarios 2 (statements) and 4
(implications).

## Sources

Style-guide anatomy (voice principle → highlights → rules with
before/after → precedence) per the quality-guideline typedef; Deming's
operational definitions (each rule's test, criterion, decision); TOGAF's
four-part principle form and BCP 14 keyword discipline, which rules 1, 2,
and 5 project into prose; the before examples are drawn from the autopsy
of the retired spec chapter (numbered principles, free-standing
anti-pattern blocks), rewritten here as counter-examples, never reused
as content.

| 3 | 2026-08-23 | update | Rule 7 added: one obligation or implication per bullet; highlights updated. |
| 4 | 2026-08-23 | update | Owner direction: decision-ledger references removed — changes stand on their own; history entries and text no longer cite numbered decisions. |

Based on the search results, I found relevant information about Julia Black's work on principles-based regulation and the FSA. Here are the key findings:

## Core Paradox and Critique

The central paradox is that unless protected by a regime enabling one in good faith to exercise judgment without fear of liability, a person will effectively act as if subject to a rule and, even worse, an unintended rule. A person subject to unpredictable liability is likely to hew to the most conservative interpretation of the principle, especially where that person would be a potential deep pocket in litigation.

## Outcomes-Focused Regulation

The FSA's focus on outcomes resembles a form of performance-based regulation. In contrast to the setting of behavioural standards or standards of conduct, performance standards specify the outcome required but leave the specific measures to achieve that outcome. However, there is no analytical correlation between using rules of a particular type (principles) and outcome-based regulation, as targets are outcomes that can be extremely precisely defined, and as such as open to gaming and 'creative compliance' as detailed rules.

## Seven Paradoxes of Principles-Based Regulation

Black identifies seven paradoxes relating to interpretation, communication, compliance, enforcement, internal management, ethics, and above all trust. Principles-based regulation can help to create trust, but the core elements of that trust have to already exist if principles-based regulation is ever to operate effectively.

content.content:
# The Simplicity Cycle Model

Based on the web content provided, here's what's explained about Dan Ward's model:

## Core Concept

Ward describes a universal framework showing how complexity affects outcomes. The model uses "a single, evolving diagram" to visualize the relationship between complexity and quality.

## The Dynamic Relationship

The key insight is that "complexity is often necessary in the development process, unnecessary complexity adds complications." The model illustrates that complexity initially improves results, but eventually becomes counterproductive—there's an optimal point beyond which added complexity diminishes value.

## The Critical Challenge

Ward identifies the core problem: "often we don't know where that point is until we pass it." This inflection point—where complexity stops helping and starts hindering—is difficult to recognize in real-time.

## Overcoming Misconceptions

A major barrier to applying the model effectively is "the idea that complexity and quality are the same." Ward argues this wrongheaded thinking prevents teams from recognizing when added complexity has become detrimental rather than beneficial.

## Practical Application

The book offers "a number of techniques for identifying the problem and fixing it," helping users understand where complexity has crossed from valuable to wasteful in their designs and processes.

##### INTERPRETIVE PARADOX
INTERPRETIVE PARADOX : PRINCIPLES CAN BE GENERAL YET  PRECISE     Principles, as explained above, are formally characterized by general, imprecise  terms.  This is meant to give flexibility.  However, in practice principles can  receive very specific interpretations.  There can be benefits: certainty is produced  through the development of an interpretive community which gives particular  content and meaning to the principles.  However, interpretive communities can  fracture, and the regulatory regime may contain several interpretive communities,  each with a different interpretation.     In particular, the interpretation which develops within the regulator may in  practice be quite specific but not necessarily well understood.  For example, the  AIM rules do not specify the proportion of shares which should be made available  on admission, but the LSE’s rule of thumb is that at least 10% of the share capital  has to be made available to the public. 81    In AIM’s case, the AIM community is  aware of this interpretation, but where interpretive communities are not as strong,  this may not be the case.  The tendency for rules to become formalized in practice  is well-observed, to the extent that a significant gap can grow between the written  word and the bureaucratic interpretation it receives.  Dan-Cohen talked of this in  terms of the ‘acoustic separation’ of law. 82   Specific interpretations may develop  for reasons of bureaucratic ease (it saves supervisors having to think every time  what conduct they should allow, enables consistent application), or because the  regulator has taken a clear policy decision, not communicated in the rules  themselves, that this is the interpretation that should be given.  Whichever the  reason, the operation of this interpretative paradox means that PBR exists only at  the formal level, and in practice can be almost indistinguishable in places from a  regime characterized by detailed rules. 83     PARADOX 2:  THE COMMUNICATIVE PARADOX : PRINCIPLES CAN FACILITATE  COMMUNICATION BUT CAN ALSO HINDER IT     In using relatively straightforward language in expressing the purpose of the rule,  PBR can facilitate communication.  Inde

The second, the  communicative paradox, is that although principles can facilitate communication  by expressing the purpose of the rule, they can hinder communication for a  number of reasons. The third paradox concerns compliance.  It is that although  PBR can provide flexibility to firms, allowing them to innovate in the ways that  they comply, in practice a lack of certainty as to what enforcers will accept as  compliance can lead firms to adopt quite conservative behaviour. 16   The fourth  paradox concerns supervision and enforcement.  Although principles can provide  flexibility to regulators in the way that they monitor and enforce the regulatory  requirements, and can save them from their own lack of foresight in the way  detailed rules cannot, regulators too can in practice develop quite conservative  interpretations and practices, particularly where there is little political support for  tough enforcement action.  The fifth paradox relates to internal management.  It is  that although principles based regulation in its substantive form relies in part on  internal compliance systems and can give them scope for expansion and  innovation, it can also overload them. COMPLIANCE PARADOX: PRINCIPLES PROVIDE SCOPE FOR  FLEXIBILITY IN COMPLIANCE YET CAN LEAD TO CONSERVATIVE AND / OR  UNIFORM BEHAVIOUR BY REGULATED FIRMS      Principles can provide flexibility for regulatees as to how they reach the outcome  that is expressed by the Principle.  However uncertainty as to the interpretation of  principles that enforcers will adopt can result in firms adopting conservative  behaviour, as if they were bound by detailed rules.  This paradox is Schwarz’s  ‘principles paradox’: that principles in practice operate in a manner akin to that  prompted by detailed rules. 92  Schwarz’s examples are drawn from common law  contexts, where the courts are the arbiters of interpretation, but there is no reason  that the paradox is avoided if the principles are applied by regulators, indeed the  second paradox of principles (the communicative paradox outlined above)  suggests that it may be exacerbated.  In this third paradox, which we may term the compliance paradox,  compliance may be either uniform or conservative or both.  So although PBR  provides flexibility in modes of compliance, in practice firms’ systems may be  quite homogenous.  This may arise because the regulator only accepts certain  practices as complying; or because firms treat guidance on practices as if it were  detailed rules.  But even where neither of these conditions obtain, close similarity  can still arise, particularly where PBR is polycentric or networked.  In polycentric  PBR, the practices of different firms are diffused (anonymously) throughout the  industry through consultants and advisors.  In sociological terms, institutional  isomorphism is transmitted and mediated through these actors.  There is no doubt  that TCF has brought considerable business for consultancy firms, ranging from  Deloittes and PwC to smaller, industry specialists and training firms, and to law  firms as well. The relationship  moves from one of directing and controlling to one based on responsibility,  mutuality and trust.  Regulators and regulatees move from a directing relationship  of telling and doing, to a relationship in which regulators communicate their goals  and expectations clearly in principles and apply those principles predictably,  regulatees adopt a self-reflective approach to the development of processes and  practices to ensure that these goals are substantively met, and, critically, both trust  each other to fulfil their side of this new regulatory bargain. PBR is based on trust that it alone cannot create,  though it can facilitate its development.  Trust in turn can help to resolve many of  the paradoxes identified above. ## Core Concept

Schauer argues that rules as entrenched generalizations are necessarily suboptimal. The generalization would by its terms control the decision even in those cases in which that generalization failed to serve its underlying justification.

## Entrenchment and Decision-Making

Rules function as entrenched generalizations, and perform better than direct references to the rule-makers' general goals in securing alignment between lawmakers' will and law-appliers' adjudicative decisions. However, this comes with trade-offs: In the context of rule-based decision-making, Schauer argues that rules as entrenched generalizations are necessarily suboptimal.

## Framework of the Book

The book includes chapters on "Rules as Generalizations," "The Entrenchment of Generalizations," "The Sources of Entrenchment," and "Decision-Making by Entrenched Generalization." Schauer makes the case for rules as devices for the allocation of power among decision-makers.

The central tension in Schauer's work is that while rules as entrenched generalizations sometimes produce suboptimal results in individual cases, they serve important functions in legal systems by constraining decision-making and allocating power among different decision-makers.

The Securities and Exchange Commission adopted a rule requiring plain English for the cover page, summary, and risk factor sections of prospectuses on January 22, 1998. This rule went into effect on October 1, 1998.

Registrants must draft the language in these sections so that, at a minimum, it substantially complies with the following plain English writing principles: active voice; short sentences; definite, concrete, everyday words; tabular presentation or "bullet" lists for complex material, whenever possible; no legal jargon or highly technical business terms; and no multiple negatives.

factors.name: Form fit: is this a rule or a standard, and does the form match the traffic?
factors.question: For each normative statement, was its content fixed in advance (a rule) or is it left to be given content at the point of application (a standard) — and does that choice match how often, and how uniformly, the situation actually arises?
factors.source: Louis Kaplow, "Rules versus Standards: An Economic Analysis," 42 Duke L.J. 557 (1992), pp. 559-60, 577, 599 — https://scholarship.law.duke.edu/dlj/vol42/iss3/2/ (full text: Harvard DASH, http://nrs.harvard.edu/urn-3:HUL.InstRepos:10611784). Kaplow: "the only distinction between rules and standards is the extent to which efforts to give content to the law are undertaken before or after individuals act" (p. 560); "the greater the frequency with which a legal command will apply, the more desirable rules tend to be relative to standards" (p. 577), because "promulgation costs are borne only once, whereas efforts to comply with and action to enforce the law may occur rarely or often."
factors.measurement: Tabulate every normative statement in the corpus. For each: (a) classify rule vs standard — can a reader decide compliance from the text alone, or must someone judge at the moment of use? (b) count actual applications in the last 30 days from the working artifacts (how many times did this statement bind a real piece of work?). Score the mismatches two ways: rules applied 0-2 times (over-promulgation — content fixed in advance for traffic that never came) and standards applied 20+ times (under-promulgation — the same judgment re-litigated every session). Report the count and percentage in each mismatch bucket, plus the total promulgation word-cost of the zero-traffic rules.
factors.why: This is the single factor that separates "too many words" from "the wrong words in the wrong form." Kaplow's result cuts against a naive verbosity diagnosis: in a shop that repeats the same activities daily, high-frequency conduct genuinely favors bright-line rules, because the cost of fixing content is paid once while the cost of re-deciding is paid every session. A healthy corpus shows rules concentrated on high-frequency, homogeneous activity and standards on rare, heterogeneous activity. A sick corpus shows the inverse — elaborate advance specification of things that happen once (migration, close-out, one-off checks) and open judgment left in the hot path that runs every day. Note Kaplow's warning that rule/standard is a choice of degree, not kind: "Deciding solely on the relevant criteria in advance may save costs for both individual actors and adjudicators, while providing individuals some guidance" (p. 600).

factors.name: Position on the discretion continuum — is the form deliberate?
factors.question: Where does each directive actually sit on the continuum from untrammeled discretion through standards, factors, presumptions, guidelines, rules-with-excuses, to rules — and does the document's label ("principle") match the form it actually takes?
factors.source: Cass R. Sunstein, "Problems with Rules," 83 Calif. L. Rev. 953 (1995), Part I, pp. 959-68 — https://scholarship.law.berkeley.edu/californialawreview/vol83/iss4/1/. Sunstein's continuum: untrammeled discretion, rules, rules with excuses, presumptions, factors, standards, guidelines, principles, analogies. Critically, on principles: "Principles are not an alternative to rules, factors, guidelines, or standards... a principle is a background notion that does not by itself cover an individual case, but is instead brought to bear on it as a relevant consideration" (p. 966); "principles tend to bear on cases without disposing of them." And on conflation: "If a standard is transparent, in the sense that there is a clear ex ante understanding of its meaning, it is a rule" (p. 965).
factors.why: Sunstein supplies the vocabulary that makes the corpus's central conflation visible and nameable. A document that defines "principle" as "a standing rule" and demands binary testability has not written principles at all — it has written rules and labelled them principles, which forecloses every other form on the continuum (presumptions, factors, guidelines with documented departure) that would carry guidance-style content. The remedy this factor points at is not "fewer words" but "more forms": a corpus that can only express rules must either over-specify or stay silent, and a system that needs to say "prefer modular design" has no grammar for it. Sunstein also disposes of the false comfort that rules eliminate judgment: "Rules do not, and indeed cannot, contain all of the instructions necessary for their own interpretation" (p. 961).
factors.measurement: Classify every directive in the corpus into Sunstein's seven forms; report the histogram. Two derived numbers matter: (1) the share of directives labelled "principle" that are in fact rules by Sunstein's test (content fully specified ex ante, decidable without weighing) — in the corpus at hand, the principle-set typedef's own definition ("A principle is a standing rule") and its statement rule ("testable: shown a piece of work, you can answer yes or no") make this share close to 100% by construction; and (2) the count of forms the corpus can express at all — a corpus that never uses a presumption, a factor list, or a documented-departure guideline has a one-form grammar. Flag any place where a guidance-style intent was abandoned because it would not fit the rule form (search the Document History and briefs for dropped or rejected principles).

factors.name: Contestability — could a competent peer shop hold the opposite?
factors.question: For each principle, can you state the credible opposite position that a serious practitioner would defend, and is anyone actually holding it?
factors.source: Jared Spool, "Creating Great Design Principles: 6 Counter-Intuitive Tests," Center Centre / UIE — https://articles.centercentre.com/creating-design-principles/ (Test #4: "Is it Something You Might Reverse in a Future Release?" — "Great principles aren't universal truths—they're contextual"). Patrick Lencioni, "Make Your Values Mean Something," Harvard Business Review, July 2002 — https://hbr.org/2002/07/make-your-values-mean-something (permission-to-play values "reflect the minimum behavioral and social standards required of any employee... by definition, they never really help distinguish a company from its competitors"; Enron's stated values were "communication, respect, integrity, and excellence"). Charlie Kindel, "Tenets" (2020) — https://blog.kindel.com/2020/02/10/tenets/ ("The most common tenet-writing mistake is creating a tenet that applies to many teams and communicates virtually no information"; "A tenet takes a stand by declaring that a team cares more about one thing than another").
factors.measurement: For each principle, write its negation as a one-line position and ask whether a named, real alternative practice holds it (cite a system, a team, or a published approach that does the opposite and survives). Score: contested (a real alternative exists and is defensible) / permission-to-play (the negation is absurd — no competent shop would hold it) / vacuous (the negation is unintelligible). Report the share in each bucket. A second, cheaper proxy: count principles whose statement contains no trade-off — no "rather than," "over," "instead of," or named cost accepted. Kindel's single-idea test gives a third: obligations per principle statement (a statement with five MUST bullets is not one stand, it is five).
factors.why: This is the strongest discriminator in the whole literature and it is cheap to apply. A principle that cannot be reversed is not guiding anything — it is announcing a baseline, and baselines belong in a one-line list, not in a four-part document with a rationale and a fitness screen. Lencioni's finding is that the bland set is not merely useless but actively corrosive: it "creat[es] cynical and dispirited employees and undermin[es] managerial credibility." Applied to an agent shop the cost is concrete — every non-contested principle compiled into every session's context spends scarce attention to buy nothing, and teaches the reader that the principle block is noise to be skimmed. Watch for the specific failure of a set whose principles are contested at the meta level ("most systems do NOT work this way") but uncontested at the point of use (given an actual artifact, no one would ever choose otherwise).

factors.name: Rejection power — how much work does this principle actually turn away?
factors.question: Shown the last N pieces of real work, how many would this principle have rejected or redirected, and can the author produce the examples?
factors.source: Jared Spool, "Creating Great Design Principles: 6 Counter-Intuitive Tests" — https://articles.centercentre.com/creating-design-principles/ (Test #2: "Does it Help You Say 'No' Most of the Time?" — strong principles "should make teams reconsider roughly two-thirds of previous design approaches"; Test #1: "Does It Come Directly From Research?" — "Everyone on your team should have a ton of examples at their fingertips"). Richard Rumelt, *Good Strategy / Bad Strategy* (Crown, 2011): the guiding policy "directs and constrains action without fully defining it"; "Fluff is a form of gibberish masquerading as strategic concepts or arguments" using "Sunday words" to "create the illusion of high-level thinking."
factors.measurement: Take the last 20-30 delivered artifacts. For each principle, count how many of them it would have rejected, and how many it actually did reject on the record (a check that failed and cited this principle, a review finding, a rewrite). Two numbers: hypothetical rejection rate and observed rejection rate. Spool's benchmark is roughly two-thirds hypothetical. A principle with an observed rejection rate of zero over the whole corpus history is inert — it has never changed an output. Also count principles whose rationale contains no concrete failure example, and — the Rumelt test — count abstract nouns per statement and check whether the statement survives substituting a plain-word paraphrase (if the paraphrase is obviously true, it was fluff).
factors.why: Rejection rate is the only direct evidence that a rule is load-bearing. It distinguishes the three failure modes cleanly: a principle that rejects nothing hypothetically is a platitude; one that rejects a lot hypothetically but nothing observably is either unenforced or routinely waived (see the unrules factor); one that rejects almost everything is mis-scoped and will be routed around. Note a structural hazard this factor exposes in the corpus at hand: its principle-set guideline forbids grounding a rationale in the product's own operational history ("it references no operational history of the product — artifacts, issues, incidents, decision records, counts"), which is precisely the evidence Spool's Test #1 demands. A rule that bans the research from the rationale guarantees that no principle can prove it came from research.

factors.name: Idea density and obligation load per unit of text
factors.question: How many separate obligations does a reader have to hold in mind to act correctly, and how much text must be traversed to find them?
factors.source: UK Office of the Parliamentary Counsel, *Drafting Guidance* (March 2024), Part 1 — https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/660407d091a320001a82b06b/2024.03.19.Drafting-guidance.pdf: "Clarity is helped by the use of short sentences. A long sentence may require the reader to keep too much in the mind. So on the whole it's best to try to stick to one idea per sentence" (1.1.11); Gowers's three principles adopted at 1.3.2 — "use no more words than are necessary; use the most familiar words; use precise and concrete words rather than vague and abstract words"; "The medium is not the message... A Bill should not draw any more attention to its own structure and mechanics than it needs to" (1.1.13); "don't create more artificial structure, such as Chapters and Parts, than you need to" (1.1.14). SEC Rule 421(d) / *A Plain English Handbook* (1998) — https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/final/33-7497.txt: active voice; short sentences; definite, concrete, everyday words; tabular or bullet presentation for complex material; no legal jargon; no multiple negatives. Plain Writing Act of 2010 (Pub. L. 111-274) §3: plain writing is "writing that is clear, concise, well-organized, and follows other best practices appropriate to the subject or field and intended audience."
factors.measurement: Per document and corpus-wide: total obligations (count normative keyword occurrences plus imperative statements); words per obligation; obligations a reader must satisfy to produce one artifact of each type (walk one real artifact and count every rule that bound it); mean sentence length and the count of sentences over 30 words; abstract-noun rate; and structural overhead — the ratio of words about the corpus's own mechanics (types, chains, renderings, compilations, load points) to words about the product or the work. Observed baseline in the corpus under analysis: 159,891 words across 115 markdown files in `basis/` produced in 26 days, 106 MUSTs, largest single process definition 6,562 words for one intake procedure. Compare against the corpus's own claimed word targets and count how many documents exceed them.
factors.why: This is the measurable core of the verbosity hypothesis, and it distinguishes length from density — a 6,000-word document with 8 obligations is navigable; a 600-word document with 25 interlocking obligations is not. The OPC's "medium is not the message" test is the sharpest instrument here: when a corpus's own machinery (typedefs, chains, compilers, renderings, fitness sets, load points) consumes more words than the subject matter it governs, the structure has become the message. That ratio is countable and it is the honest form of the "too verbose" complaint: the problem is not that sentences are long but that a reader must assemble an obligation from four documents at three levels of a chain.

factors.name: Escape-hatch accounting — count the unrules, and check whether they are checked
factors.question: For every obligation, what mechanisms exist to lift it — waiver, accepted gap, accepted tradeoff, self-asserted pass, exception, deferral — who may invoke them, and is invoking one as scrutinised as imposing the obligation was?
factors.source: Cary Coglianese, Gabriel Scheffler & Daniel E. Walters, "Unrules," 73 Stan. L. Rev. 885 (2021) — https://review.law.stanford.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2021/04/Coglianese-et-al.-73-Stan.-L.-Rev.-885.pdf: "for every one of these rules, there are also unrules nearby... the decisions that regulators make to lift or limit the scope of a regulatory obligation through, for instance, waivers, exemptions, or exceptions" (p. 885); "A regulatory system can be understood only as the net effects of both its rules and its unrules" (p. 892); "current administrative law tends to impose greater constraints on government agencies' ability to impose obligations than on their ability to alleviate them... Swaths of administrative discretion to alleviate or eliminate obligations remain effectively unchecked" (p. 892). Cass Sunstein, "Problems with Rules," 83 Calif. L. Rev. 953, 1000-01: "once it is decided that a single exception will be allowed, it is always open, in principle, to decide that another exception should be made too... the line between case-by-case judgments and rule-following becomes thin."
factors.measurement: Build the unrule register: grep the corpus and the working artifacts for accepted gap, accepted tradeoff, exception, waiver, deferred, out of scope for now, not repaired in this amendment, and for self-asserted pass tables. For each entry record: which obligation it lifts, who invoked it, whether a different role approved it, whether it expires, and whether it was ever revisited. Report (a) unrules per obligation, (b) the share invoked by the same role the obligation constrains, (c) the share with no expiry and no owner, (d) elapsed time since each was filed. Then the asymmetry test: compare the process weight of imposing an obligation (draft, guideline, fitness set, independent judge, owner approval) against the process weight of lifting one in practice. In the corpus at hand, the founding principle set's own fitness screen is a table of self-asserted "pass" verdicts followed by an "Accepted tradeoffs" section in which the author records known violations of the set's own rules and declines to repair them — imposition took a multi-step authoring process with an independent judge; alleviation took a paragraph.
factors.why: This is the decisive structural factor and the literature is unambiguous about it: a rule system's real content is rules minus unrules, and unrules are systematically less governed because nobody builds process around making things easier. The Coglianese finding predicts exactly the pattern to look for — not open defiance but a quiet parallel channel of relief that nobody audits. Two specific forms matter in an agent-run shop: (1) the maker stamping approval or asserting a fitness pass on its own output, which collapses the separation the rule was built to create, and (2) the tooling bypass (editing an artifact with sed when a tool exists to write it), which is an unrule at the mechanical layer. Both are countable from history. Sunstein adds the dynamic: once one exception stands unrepaired, refusing the next one requires an argument nobody has, so the unrule register grows monotonically unless something forces reconciliation.

factors.name: Normative-keyword discipline: conformance object, gradation, and necessity
factors.question: Does each MUST identify who must conform and what observable behavior would violate it, is the keyword reserved for cases where deviation actually breaks something, and does the corpus use the full gradation or has MUST become the only voice?
factors.source: S. Bradner, RFC 2119 / BCP 14, "Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels" (1997), §6 — https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119.txt: "Imperatives of the type defined in this memo must be used with care and sparingly. In particular, they MUST only be used where it is actually required for interoperation or to limit behavior which has potential for causing harm (e.g., limiting retransmissions)... they must not be used to try to impose a particular method on implementors where the method is not required for interoperability." B. Leiba, RFC 8174 (2017) — https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8174.txt: the keywords have their defined meaning "only when, and only when, they appear in all capitals." W3C QA guidance on RFC 2119 keywords — https://www.w3.org/wiki/RfcKeywords: keywords should attach to a defined conformance object performing a specified operation; a specification should establish a conformance model before deploying them. OASIS Keyword Guidelines — https://www.oasis-open.org/policies-guidelines/keyword-guidelines/.
factors.measurement: For each capitalised keyword: (a) name the conformance object — the role or agent that must conform — and reject any occurrence where it is unnamed or is a document rather than an actor (W3C: prefer "X MUST do Y," not "X MUST be Y"); (b) state the observable violation; (c) apply RFC 2119 §6's own test — is deviation actually harmful or interoperability-breaking, or is this a preferred method? Report the MUST:SHOULD:MAY ratio and the share of MUSTs that fail the §6 test. Observed baseline in the corpus under analysis: 106 MUST, 5 SHOULD, 13 MAY across `basis/` — a 21:1 MUST:SHOULD ratio, meaning the gradation the convention exists to provide is essentially unused.
factors.why: The verdict the literature supports is narrower and more useful than "RFC 2119 doesn't belong outside interop." W3C, OASIS and many non-IETF bodies use BCP 14 soundly. What makes a use sound is the conformance model: a named actor, a specified operation, and an observable violation. What makes it unsound is importing the capitals as a tone of authority with no conformance object — which produces documents that read as specifications but cannot be conformance-tested, and whose authors then invent in-document fitness screens to compensate. The MUST:SHOULD ratio is the cheapest single diagnostic in this whole list: RFC 2119 §6 says use them sparingly and reserve MUST for harm or interoperability, so a near-total absence of SHOULD is direct evidence that the keyword is doing rhetorical rather than normative work. A corpus whose purpose is improving an agent's judgment and which has 106 absolute requirements and five recommendations has no register in which to say "here is the default, depart from it with reason" — the exact register Sunstein's guidelines and Kaplow's partial specification occupy.

factors.name: Coverage of the artifact versus coverage of the procedure
factors.question: What share of the corpus describes what a good built thing looks like, as against who does what, in what order, with which check?
factors.source: Richard Rumelt, *Good Strategy / Bad Strategy* (2011) — the kernel is diagnosis, guiding policy, and coherent action; bad strategy's hallmarks are fluff, failure to face the challenge, mistaking goals for strategy, and bad objectives (summary: https://www.alexmurrell.co.uk/summaries/richard-rumelt-good-strategy-bad-strategy). TOGAF Standard, Architecture Principles — a good set must be "Complete: every potentially important principle governing the management of information and technology for the organization is defined" and "Robust: enable good quality decisions about architectures and plans to be made" (https://pubs.opengroup.org/architecture/togaf92-doc/arch/chap20.html; open mirror: https://coe.qualiware.com/resources/togaf/9-1/part3-admguide/architecture-principles/). Jeff Bezos, 2017 Letter to Shareholders — https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/company-news/2017-letter-to-shareholders: "high standards are teachable," requiring that people can "recognize what excellence looks like in a domain" and hold a realistic expectation of scope.
factors.measurement: Classify every directive as artifact-quality (a property of the thing produced: its structure, its interfaces, its failure behavior, its readability) or process-quality (who performs, in what order, with what record, checked by whom). Report the ratio per principle set and corpus-wide. Then the coverage test: pick five questions a maker would actually ask while building — how should this be decomposed, what belongs behind an interface, how should errors surface, when is duplication acceptable, what does done mean for this scenario — and count how many the corpus answers. In the corpus at hand, the six implementation principles are `built-to-the-scenario`, `effect-shown`, `effect-not-mechanism`, `nothing-lost`, `knowable-from-the-record`, `cost-on-the-initiative`: all six govern scope, evidence, record-keeping and accounting; none states a property of well-built software.
factors.why: This is where the form constraint bites hardest and where the damage is largest. "Use modular design" is a standard in Kaplow's sense and a principle in Sunstein's — it bears on cases without disposing of them — so a corpus that admits only binary-testable standing rules cannot express it and will silently drop it. The result is a principle set that is complete about procedure and empty about product, which TOGAF's "Complete" criterion would fail and which Rumelt would call mistaking activity for strategy. Bezos's formulation names the operational consequence precisely: standards are teachable only if the learner can recognise what excellence looks like in the domain. A corpus that never describes a good artifact cannot teach the standard for one, so every judgment about built quality falls back on the one human — which is also the mechanism behind the bottleneck.

factors.name: Independent-application agreement
factors.question: Given the same artifact and the same rule, do two independent readers reach the same verdict?
factors.source: Colin S. Diver, "The Optimal Precision of Administrative Rules," 93 Yale L.J. 65 (1983) — the three criteria for rule precision: transparency (words with well-understood meanings), accessibility (applicable to concrete situations without excessive difficulty), and congruence (the substantive result matches the policy it serves). W. Edwards Deming's operational definitions (*Out of the Crisis*, 1986): a definition is operational only if two people applying it to the same thing get the same answer — a test the corpus's own guideline invokes by naming a test, criterion and decision for each rule. US federal plain-language practice, "Test for understanding" — https://digital.gov/guides/plain-language. Julia Black, "Forms and Paradoxes of Principles Based Regulation," LSE Law, Society and Economy Working Paper 13/2008, pp. 22-24 (the interpretive paradox) — https://www.lse.ac.uk/law/research/working-paper-series/2007-08/WPS2008-13-Black.pdf.
factors.measurement: Run the test rather than asserting it. Take 10 rules and 10 real artifacts; have two independent fresh-context readers (for an agent shop: two fresh agent sessions loading only the rule and the artifact, no shared transcript) return a yes/no verdict plus the clause they relied on. Report the agreement rate per rule and the clause-citation agreement rate. Rules under ~80% agreement are standards wearing a rule's clothes — the content is being supplied at application time, by whoever happens to be reading. Cross-check against history: count the clarification exchanges each rule has generated with the authority, which is the same signal measured in human time.
factors.why: Every other factor here is a proxy for this one, and it is the only one that produces evidence rather than opinion. It settles the judgment-dependence question empirically: a rule the corpus calls binary-testable but on which two readers disagree is generating exactly the interpretation cost Kaplow assigns to standards while paying the promulgation cost of a rule — the worst cell of the matrix. Black's interpretive paradox explains what happens next and is worth watching for directly: in practice a specific interpretation forms inside whoever applies the rule most, it is never written down, and "a significant gap can grow between the written word and the bureaucratic interpretation it receives." In an agent shop with one human, that interpretation lives in the human's head, which is precisely how dense rules convert into demands on the one person who can resolve them.

factors.name: Check burden and the enforcement budget
factors.question: What fraction of total effort goes into checking rather than making, is each check traceable to the clause it enforces, and was the recurring cost of the check counted when the rule was adopted?
factors.source: Louis Kaplow, 42 Duke L.J. 557, 572-77 (enforcement costs are the recurring term; "Promulgation costs are incurred once. In contrast, enforcement costs may be incurred repeatedly"). TOGAF's "Robust" criterion: principles should "enable good quality decisions... and enforceable policies and standards to be created" — enforceability is a property to be designed, not assumed (https://coe.qualiware.com/resources/togaf/9-1/part3-admguide/architecture-principles/). Julia Black, LSE WP 13/2008, the enforcement paradox (pp. 29-31): principles "need enforcement to give them credibility but over-enforcement can lead to their demise" — under heavy enforcement, "PBR is likely to transform as firms seek the comfort of detailed rules." Dan Ward, *The Simplicity Cycle* (HarperBusiness, 2015) — http://www.thedanward.com/the-simplicity-cycle/: complexity raises goodness up to an inflection point and lowers it after, and "often we don't know where that point is until we pass it."
factors.measurement: From session records and cost rows, compute the ratio of effort spent on checks, screens, reviews and re-checks to effort spent producing the artifact being checked. Count check steps per process definition and the number of distinct checks one artifact passes end to end. Count checks that cannot cite the clause they enforce (the corpus's own founding set says such a check "has no standing") and checks that have never failed — a check with a 100% historical pass rate is either redundant with the making step or is being performed pro forma. Plot the trend over the 26 days: rising check-to-make ratio with flat or falling delivered output is the Simplicity Cycle past its inflection.
factors.why: The recurring cost of a rule is its check, and it is the cost systems reliably fail to budget because it is paid later and by someone else. This factor tests the claim that a design principle about being explicit was read as an operating obligation and multiplied: if a single clause requiring that good be defined up front has generated a check step at the end of every process, the clause's promulgation cost was one paragraph and its enforcement cost is a permanent tax on every activity forever. Kaplow's asymmetry says that is exactly the cost you must count before adopting the clause, not after. Black's enforcement paradox supplies the second-order effect worth watching: heavy checking does not produce compliance, it produces demand for more detailed rules, because makers under unpredictable review seek the safety of specification — which is a self-reinforcing loop from checks to corpus growth to more checks.

factors.name: Set-level properties: size, conflict handling, and stability
factors.question: How many principles are there, does the set state how to act when two conflict, and how often does it change?
factors.source: TOGAF Standard, Architecture Principles (The Open Group) — https://pubs.opengroup.org/architecture/togaf92-doc/arch/chap20.html: the five criteria for a good set are Understandable, Robust, Complete, Consistent and Stable; "Consistent: Strict adherence to one principle may require a loose interpretation of another principle... the set of principles must be expressed in a way that allows a balance of interpretations"; "Stable: principles should be enduring, yet able to accommodate changes"; "Many organizations prefer to define only high-level principles, and to limit the number to between 10 and 20"; and the warning that "A poor set of principles will quickly become disused, and the resultant architectures, policies, and standards will appear arbitrary or self-serving, and thus lack credibility." The four-part form (Name, Statement, Rationale, Implications) with the drafting caution to "avoid ambiguous words in the Name and in the Statement such as: 'support', 'open', 'consider'."
factors.measurement: Count principles per set and across all sets combined (the reader of a session prompt faces the union, not one set). Check for a stated conflict rule — what a maker does when two principles pull opposite ways — and count the documented instances where a conflict was actually resolved. Measure stability as versions per set per month and clauses changed per month; a set on version 7 within four weeks is not yet stable in TOGAF's sense, and everything compiled from it was produced under a different rule. Also count cross-references between sets and the depth of the chain a reader must walk to resolve one obligation.
factors.why: TOGAF's "Consistent" criterion is the most consequential line in the framework for this corpus and it is routinely mis-cited. TOGAF explicitly expects that honouring one principle will require loosening another, and requires the set to be written so that a balance of interpretations is possible. That is incompatible with a construction that demands every statement be decidable yes/no on one artifact in isolation: binary testability per statement plus no conflict rule means conflicts surface as failed checks with no legitimate resolution path, which is precisely the pressure that produces accepted-tradeoff waivers. Citing TOGAF for "testable" while dropping "allows a balance of interpretations" is a partial adoption that inverts the source's intent — and it is checkable, because the corpus names TOGAF in its own fitness screen.

factors.name: Definition hygiene — do defined terms earn their keep?
factors.question: Is each defined term load-bearing, is its label honest about its meaning, and does defining it reduce or increase what a reader must hold?
factors.source: UK OPC, *Drafting Guidance* (March 2024), Part 4.1 — https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/660407d091a320001a82b06b/2024.03.19.Drafting-guidance.pdf: "Avoid labels that are misleading" (4.1.4); "Where possible avoid bland terms such as 'the relevant person'... Try instead to use a label that gives the reader some clue as to what it means" (4.1.5); "Think carefully before using acronyms... Initials may be shorter but this often comes at a cost to the reader who has to decode what they stand for" (4.1.6); "Don't make a definition do too much... it is usually best to avoid using a definition to make operative provision" (4.1.8-9); "Defining terms 'unless the context otherwise requires' is generally unhelpful" (4.1.18). Bryan A. Garner, *Legal Writing in Plain English* (3rd ed., University of Chicago Press, 2023) — https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/L/bo199200593.html: draft for the ordinary reader, not for a hypothetical reviewer.
factors.measurement: For each glossary term and schema element: count its uses outside its own definition; count uses where an ordinary word would carry the same meaning; and flag every definition that smuggles an obligation into it (OPC 4.1.8 — a definition that imposes a duty should have been an operative provision). Compute the decode cost of one working sentence: take five representative sentences from process definitions and count how many defined terms a reader must already know to parse each. Terms used fewer than three times outside their definition are candidates for deletion; sentences requiring four or more defined-term lookups are candidates for rewriting in plain words.
factors.why: A vocabulary requirement — use the defined term where one exists — is cheap to write and expensive to read, and it compounds with every new term. Each definition adds a lookup to every sentence that uses it, so a corpus that keeps coining terms raises the fixed cost of reading anything, which is the mechanism by which documents become dense without becoming long. The OPC's warning about definitions doing operative work is directly relevant to a corpus built on typedefs: when the type definition carries obligations, the reader must read the type to know the rules, and the rules are no longer where the reader is looking. This factor is also the cleanest way to test whether a house style has drifted into what Rumelt calls Sunday words — count how many defined terms could be replaced by ordinary English without loss.

factors.name: Provenance and fidelity of adopted external forms
factors.question: Where the corpus cites an external standard, does it adopt the form as its source defines it, and is any departure recorded as a deliberate, reasoned gap?
factors.source: The sources as they define themselves: TOGAF's five set-level criteria including "allows a balance of interpretations" (https://pubs.opengroup.org/architecture/togaf92-doc/arch/chap20.html); RFC 2119 §6's own limits on its keywords (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119.txt) and RFC 8174's capitalisation rule (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8174.txt); Spool's six tests in full (https://articles.centercentre.com/creating-design-principles/); Lencioni's four value types, of which permission-to-play is only one (https://hbr.org/2002/07/make-your-values-mean-something); Rumelt's kernel requiring a diagnosis before any guiding policy.
factors.measurement: For each external source the corpus names, put the source's own criteria in one column and the corpus's rendering of them in the next, and mark each as adopted, narrowed, inverted or dropped. Score fidelity as the share adopted intact and require a recorded justification for each narrowing. In the corpus at hand this is a short and revealing table: TOGAF's Understandable/Complete/Consistent are collapsed into "statement testable," with Robust and Stable dropped and Consistent's balance-of-interpretations clause inverted; Spool's six tests are reduced to Test #2 alone, with Test #1 (comes from research) contradicted by the ban on product history in rationales and Test #4 (reversibility) absent; BCP 14 is adopted without the §6 necessity limit; and the corpus adds a criterion of its own — "implies at least one practice and at least one check" — which appears in none of the four cited sources.
factors.why: A corpus that claims external grounding buys credibility on that claim, so fidelity is directly auditable and cheap to audit. The pattern to look for is not fabrication but selective adoption that happens to license what the author already wanted: keeping the criteria that push toward specification, dropping the ones that push toward flexibility, and adding a home-grown criterion presented in the same breath as the cited four. That last move is the one to flag hardest — "implies at least one check" is the clause that converts a set of principles into a generator of process mass, and it is the one clause in the screen with no external parent. A reviewer should treat any criterion in a fitness screen that cannot be traced to a named source as a bespoke structure requiring the same justification the corpus demands elsewhere.

factors.name: Promulgation-to-delivery ratio and the trust the regime presupposes
factors.question: How much definition has been produced per unit of the thing the definitions exist to produce, and does the regime require a level of trust or shared interpretation that does not yet exist?
factors.source: Dan Ward, *The Simplicity Cycle* (HarperBusiness, 2015) — http://www.thedanward.com/the-simplicity-cycle/ and *FIRE: How Fast, Inexpensive, Restrained, and Elegant Methods Ignite Innovation* (HarperBusiness, 2014): complexity raises goodness only up to an inflection point, and the inflection is usually recognised after it is crossed. Julia Black, LSE WP 13/2008, the trust paradox (pp. 35-36): "there has to be a high level of trust between all the participants... for PBR... to operate at all. PBR can help this relationship develop; but it needs it to exist before PBR can even begin to work... Without trust, PBR will never be operationalised; it will exist only in the text of the rule books, not in the way they are implemented." Jeff Bezos, 2017 Letter to Shareholders — https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/company-news/2017-letter-to-shareholders: unrealistic beliefs about scope "kill high standards," and a great six-pager takes "a week or more" of rewriting.
factors.measurement: Compute definition words per delivered unit of product output (features shipped, scenarios built, lines of working software), tracked weekly so the trend is visible; and definition words per definition word — the share of new corpus that governs other corpus rather than the product. Observed baseline in the corpus under analysis: ~160,000 definition words in 26 days and zero software built, with a fifth restart under consideration. Second measure, for the trust half: count the points in the flow where a single human must decide, the mean queue time at each, and the share of total elapsed time spent waiting on that one person. Third: count how many rules exist because a previous rule was not trusted to hold — checks on checks, renderings verified against sources verified against typedefs.
factors.why: This is the whole-system factor that catches what per-rule scoring misses, and it converts the restart question into a measurement. Ward's inflection is observable in the ratio's trend rather than its level: a corpus still buying delivery with definition is pre-inflection; one where added definition tracks with falling delivery has crossed it. Black's trust paradox names the deeper trap and it transfers to agent shops with unusual force: a regime built on judgment requires that the judge be trusted, and every check added because the maker was not trusted is an admission that the regime's precondition is missing — so the regime compensates with more specification, which raises the reading cost, which degrades judgment, which justifies more checking. A corpus in that loop cannot be fixed rule by rule, because each rule is locally defensible; the ratio is the only place the loop is visible.

input.key_sources:
PRIMARY — regulatory theory (the rules/standards question, directly on point):
• Louis Kaplow, "Rules versus Standards: An Economic Analysis," 42 Duke Law Journal 557 (1992). Full text: https://scholarship.law.duke.edu/dlj/vol42/iss3/2/ and Harvard DASH http://nrs.harvard.edu/urn-3:HUL.InstRepos:10611784. The core answer to the assignment's central question. A rule fixes content ex ante; a standard leaves content to be supplied ex post. Rules cost more to promulgate once; standards cost more to interpret and enforce every time. Therefore: "the greater the frequency with which a legal command will apply, the more desirable rules tend to be relative to standards" (p. 577). Bright lines are correct for frequent, homogeneous conduct; open standards are correct for rare, heterogeneous conduct that cannot be cheaply anticipated (pp. 599-600). Complexity is a separate axis from rule-ness (Part II).
• Cass R. Sunstein, "Problems with Rules," 83 California Law Review 953 (1995). https://scholarship.law.berkeley.edu/californialawreview/vol83/iss4/1/. Supplies the continuum — untrammeled discretion, rules, rules with excuses, presumptions, factors, standards, guidelines, principles, analogies — and the definitions that let a reviewer classify each directive. Decisive for the principle-versus-rule question: "Principles are not an alternative to rules, factors, guidelines, or standards... a principle is a background notion that does not by itself cover an individual case, but is instead brought to bear on it as a relevant consideration" (p. 966); "principles tend to bear on cases without disposing of them." Also: "If a standard is transparent... it is a rule" (p. 965), and "Rules do not, and indeed cannot, contain all of the instructions necessary for their own interpretation" (p. 961).
• Cary Coglianese, Gabriel Scheffler & Daniel E. Walters, "Unrules," 73 Stanford Law Review 885 (2021). https://review.law.stanford.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2021/04/Coglianese-et-al.-73-Stan.-L.-Rev.-885.pdf. The waiver question, empirically. "A regulatory system can be understood only as the net effects of both its rules and its unrules" (p. 892), and the systematic asymmetry: imposing an obligation is heavily processed, lifting one is not.
• Julia Black, "Forms and Paradoxes of Principles Based Regulation," LSE Law, Society and Economy Working Paper 13/2008. https://www.lse.ac.uk/law/research/working-paper-series/2007-08/WPS2008-13-Black.pdf (also Capital Markets Law Journal 3(4):425, 2008). Seven paradoxes — interpretation, communication, compliance, enforcement, internal management, ethics, trust. The interpretive paradox (an unwritten specific interpretation forms inside whoever applies the rule most) and the trust paradox (principles-based regimes need the trust they are meant to create) are the two that transfer most directly.
• Colin S. Diver, "The Optimal Precision of Administrative Rules," 93 Yale Law Journal 65 (1983) — transparency, accessibility, congruence. Frederick Schauer, *Playing by the Rules* (Oxford, 1991) — rules as entrenched generalizations that are necessarily suboptimal in some cases and valuable for exactly that reason. Isaac Ehrlich & Richard Posner, "An Economic Analysis of Legal Rulemaking," 3 J. Legal Studies 257 (1974) — over- and under-inclusiveness.

PRIMARY — principle and tenet craft:
• TOGAF Standard, Architecture Principles (The Open Group). https://pubs.opengroup.org/architecture/togaf92-doc/arch/chap20.html (open mirror: https://coe.qualiware.com/resources/togaf/9-1/part3-admguide/architecture-principles/). Four-part form (Name, Statement, Rationale, Implications); five set-level criteria — Understandable, Robust, Complete, Consistent, Stable — of which Consistent expressly requires that the set "allows a balance of interpretations"; 10-20 principles typical; "A poor set of principles will quickly become disused."
• Jared Spool, "Creating Great Design Principles: 6 Counter-Intuitive Tests," Center Centre/UIE. https://articles.centercentre.com/creating-design-principles/. Comes from research; helps you say no most of the time; distinguishes you from competitors; is something you might reverse in a future release; re-evaluated per project; meaning constantly tested against real work.
• Patrick Lencioni, "Make Your Values Mean Something," Harvard Business Review, July 2002. https://hbr.org/2002/07/make-your-values-mean-something. Core / aspirational / permission-to-play / accidental; permission-to-play values "never really help distinguish a company"; bland values are "highly destructive."
• Richard Rumelt, *Good Strategy / Bad Strategy* (Crown Business, 2011). The kernel — diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent action — with the guiding policy that "directs and constrains action without fully defining it." "Fluff is a form of gibberish masquerading as strategic concepts or arguments," using "Sunday words" to create "the illusion of high-level thinking."
• Charlie Kindel, "Tenets" (2020). https://blog.kindel.com/2020/02/10/tenets/. Amazon practice: minimal cover of single-idea tenets, "unless you know better ones," a tenet "takes a stand by declaring that a team cares more about one thing than another," and the commonest mistake is a tenet that "applies to many teams and communicates virtually no information."
• Jeff Bezos, 2017 Letter to Shareholders. https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/company-news/2017-letter-to-shareholders. Narratively structured six-pagers; "high standards are teachable"; wrong expectations about scope kill high standards.

PRIMARY — drafting and plain language:
• UK Office of the Parliamentary Counsel, *Drafting Guidance*, March 2024. https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/660407d091a320001a82b06b/2024.03.19.Drafting-guidance.pdf. Gowers's three principles at 1.3.2; one idea per sentence (1.1.11); "The medium is not the message" (1.1.13-14); office policy to avoid legislative "shall" (1.2.9); definitions guidance at Part 4.1.
• Plain Writing Act of 2010, Pub. L. 111-274, §3 — plain writing is "clear, concise, well-organized, and follows other best practices appropriate to the subject or field and intended audience." https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-111publ274/html/PLAW-111publ274.htm. Federal guidance: https://digital.gov/guides/plain-language.
• SEC Rule 421(d) and *A Plain English Handbook* (1998) — six measurable drafting principles, applied deliberately to only three sections of a prospectus. https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/final/33-7497.txt.
• Bryan A. Garner, *Legal Writing in Plain English* (3rd ed., University of Chicago Press, 2023). https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/L/bo199200593.html.

PRIMARY — normative keywords:
• S. Bradner, RFC 2119 / BCP 14 (1997). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119.txt. §6: "Imperatives of the type defined in this memo must be used with care and sparingly. In particular, they MUST only be used where it is actually required for interoperation or to limit behavior which has potential for causing harm... they must not be used to try to impose a particular method on implementors where the method is not required for interoperability."
• B. Leiba, RFC 8174 (2017). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8174.txt. Keywords bind only in all capitals.
• W3C, RfcKeywords. https://www.w3.org/wiki/RfcKeywords. Keywords attach to a conformance object performing an operation; establish a conformance model first; prefer "X MUST do Y" over "X MUST be Y." OASIS Keyword Guidelines: https://www.oasis-open.org/policies-guidelines/keyword-guidelines/.

SIMPLICITY:
• Dan Ward, *The Simplicity Cycle* (HarperBusiness, 2015) and *FIRE* (HarperBusiness, 2014). http://www.thedanward.com/the-simplicity-cycle/. Complexity raises goodness to an inflection point and lowers it after; the inflection is usually recognised only after it is crossed.

CORPUS MEASUREMENTS TAKEN WHILE DERIVING THESE FACTORS (baselines a reviewer can re-run):
159,891 words across 115 markdown files under /home/vscode/rebaseline/basis, produced in 26 days, with no software built. Normative keywords: 106 MUST, 5 SHOULD, 13 MAY — a 21:1 MUST:SHOULD ratio. Principle counts: 9 founding, 6 architecture, 6 implementation. All six implementation principles (`built-to-the-scenario`, `effect-shown`, `effect-not-mechanism`, `nothing-lost`, `knowable-from-the-record`, `cost-on-the-initiative`) govern scope, evidence and record-keeping; none states a property of well-built software. /home/vscode/rebaseline/basis/architecture-principles.md and /home/vscode/rebaseline/basis/implementation-principles.md each end in a self-asserted fitness screen whose rows read "pass"; /home/vscode/rebaseline/basis/principles.md follows its screen with an "Accepted tradeoffs" section recording six known violations of the set's own rules, declined for repair. /home/vscode/rebaseline/basis/guidelines/principle-set.md rule 3 forbids grounding a rationale in the product's own operational history. The screen's criteria cite TOGAF, Spool, Rumelt and Lencioni, plus one criterion — "implies ≥1 practice and ≥1 check" — traceable to no cited source.
input.cautions:
WHERE THE LITERATURE DISAGREES WITH ITSELF

1. Rules versus standards has no winner, and the strongest sources say so. Kaplow's frequency result argues *for* bright-line rules wherever conduct repeats — and an agent shop repeats its activities constantly, so a reviewer who applies this literature carelessly can arrive at "write more rules, not fewer." The honest reading is that Kaplow prices form against traffic; he does not license either form in the abstract. Anyone using these factors to argue that the corpus is over-ruled must show low application frequency per rule, not merely high word count. Diver and Ehrlich/Posner reach compatible but differently weighted conclusions; Schauer argues that rules earn their keep *because* they produce wrong answers in some cases, which cuts directly against a fitness screen that treats any counterexample as a defect.

2. TOGAF is contested as a source. Its five criteria are themselves vague standards, not tests, and its "Complete" criterion — every potentially important principle defined — is an engine of corpus bloat that a shop in this condition should probably reject outright rather than cite. TOGAF has a substantial practitioner critique as heavyweight and ceremony-producing. Citing it for authority while the diagnosis is "too much ceremony" deserves a second look; the useful parts here are the four-part form, the 10-20 heuristic, and the balance-of-interpretations clause, not the framework.

3. The design-principle sources (Spool, Lencioni, Kindel, Rumelt, Bezos) are practitioner lore, not evidence. None is empirically validated; Spool's "two-thirds" is a rule of thumb, not a finding; Amazon's tenets and six-pagers are known mainly through secondhand accounts and one shareholder letter. They are sharp instruments for detecting platitudes and they converge remarkably across independent authors, which is the best warrant available — but they are also aimed at a different target than governance. Spool's reversibility test is designed to find principles that differentiate a *product*; applied to a safety or integrity constraint it misfires, since "don't lose data" is permission-to-play and should still be written down. Use contestability to decide what belongs in a compiled prompt block, not to decide what is true.

4. RFC 2119 outside interoperability is not settled as unsound. W3C, OASIS and many non-IETF bodies use BCP 14 deliberately and defensibly, and §6 is itself advice inside a document about IETF practice. The defensible finding is narrower: the convention presupposes a conformance model — a named conformance object, a specified operation, an observable violation — and where that model is absent the capitals convey authority without conveying testability. A 21:1 MUST:SHOULD ratio is good evidence of that failure. "MUST/SHOULD/MAY cannot be used in judgment documents" is not a claim the sources support.

5. Black's paradoxes cut both ways and should not be used as a one-sided brief. Her central point is that switching from principles to detailed rules does not escape the failure modes: "many of these paradoxes are not necessarily avoided by using detailed rules instead of principles." Gaming, creative compliance and conservative over-application occur under both forms. Anyone proposing a second restart toward looser guidance should expect the interpretive paradox to reappear in the new corpus within weeks.

WHERE THIS LITERATURE FITS THIS SHOP BADLY

6. The cost model does not transfer intact. Kaplow's arithmetic assumes promulgation is expensive and slow, individuals are informed once and remember, and adjudication is scarce. In an agent-run shop all three invert: promulgation is nearly free and extremely fast — which is *why* 160,000 words appeared in 26 days and is itself the best available explanation for corpus mass without any theory of verbosity; "becoming informed" is not amortised at all but re-paid in full every session, from a hard context budget; and checking is cheap to invoke but consumes the same scarce budget. The net effect is that the cost the legal literature treats as one-time (promulgation) is nearly zero here, while the cost it treats as recurring (informing the actor) is both recurring and hard-capped. That argues for a much smaller total corpus than any legal analogy would suggest, and it argues for it on grounds the legal literature never had to consider. Treat the frameworks as vocabulary and diagnostic structure; do not import their conclusions.

7. Plain-language evidence is about human readers. The comprehension research behind Gowers, the Plain Writing Act and SEC Rule 421 measures ordinary people reading prose. Whether short sentences and familiar words improve *model* compliance is a different question with a much thinner evidence base; known model-specific effects — position and recency sensitivity, instruction conflict, degradation with context length — have no counterpart in the plain-language canon. Readability metrics are reasonable heuristics and good for detecting drift, but a reviewer should not present a Flesch score as evidence about agent behavior. The one measurement in the factor list that does transfer cleanly is independent-application agreement, because it tests the actual reader.

8. Several factors measure the corpus by its own instruments, which is exactly the failure they are meant to detect. "Count the checks," "count the accepted gaps," "score fidelity to cited sources" all invite a corpus to respond by adding a check that counts checks. Campbell's law applies with full force to a system that defines itself: any measure adopted as a target stops measuring. Run these factors once, as a diagnosis, by someone who does not own the corpus; do not operationalise them into standing screens inside it.

9. The measurements offered are countable but not neutral. Classifying a directive as rule versus standard, or artifact-quality versus process-quality, is a judgment call, and reasonable reviewers will differ at the margin — which is the same problem this whole analysis is about. Report classification disagreement rather than a single clean number, and prefer the factors with hard counts (MUST:SHOULD ratio, unrules per obligation, words per obligation, definition words per delivered unit, two-reader agreement rate) when the conclusion has to carry weight in a restart decision.

10. Nothing in this literature speaks to the specific mechanism of a system that writes its own governing documents at machine speed with one human approver. The closest analogues are Black's trust paradox and Coglianese's asymmetry, and both are about institutions with many participants and years of feedback.
